Paulicians
paul-ISH-unz
noun (early-medieval dualist sect)
Seventh-to-ninth-century dualist Christian sect of Armenia and the eastern Byzantine Empire; named either for the apostle Paul (whom they particularly revered) or for Paul of Samosata (whom some early sources identified as their founder). Substantively gnostic-dualist; ancestral or related to the Bogomils and ultimately to the medieval Cathari.

📖 Biblical Definition

Seventh-to-ninth-century dualist Christian sect of Armenia and the eastern Byzantine Empire. The name Paulicians (Greek Pauliciani) is derived either from the apostle Paul (whom they particularly revered, treating his epistles as authoritative scripture while rejecting much of the OT) or from Paul of Samosata (the third-century adoptionist whom some early Byzantine sources identified as their founder; the etymology is contested in modern scholarship). The movement is traditionally traced to Constantine of Mananali (mid-seventh century), who founded the sect in Armenia substantially under the influence of earlier Marcionite and Manichaean ideas. The Paulicians spread substantially across Armenia, Asia Minor, and Thrace through the late seventh, eighth, and ninth centuries; were intermittently tolerated and intermittently persecuted by Byzantine emperors; were forcibly transplanted in large numbers to Thrace under Emperor John Tzimiskes (970) and Emperor Constantine VII (mid-tenth century), where they substantially contributed to the formation of the later Bogomil movement. The Paulicians' principal distinctives included: (1) dualist cosmology (two principles; the evil principle as creator of the material world and identified with the OT God; the good principle as the spiritual God of the NT); (2) docetic Christology (Christ as adopted at baptism, not as eternal Son in real material incarnation); (3) rejection of OT; (4) rejection of orthodox sacraments and church hierarchy; (5) special veneration of Paul; (6) rejection of icons and physical aids to worship. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the Paulicians as the substantive eastern-medieval ancestor of the Bogomil-Catharist dualist tradition that continued through to the medieval Western Albigenses.

PAULICIANS, n. (early-medieval dualist sect; 7th-9th-c. Armenia and eastern Byzantine Empire) Name derived from apostle Paul (revered, NT epistles authoritative) or Paul of Samosata (third-century adoptionist some early sources identified as founder; etymology contested). Traced to Constantine of Mananali (mid-7th c.) in Armenia under influence of earlier Marcionite and Manichaean ideas. Spread across Armenia, Asia Minor, Thrace through late 7th, 8th, 9th c.; intermittently tolerated and persecuted by Byzantine emperors. Forcibly transplanted to Thrace under John Tzimiskes (970) and Constantine VII (mid-10th c.); contributed to later Bogomil movement formation. Distinctives: (1) dualist cosmology; (2) docetic Christology (Christ adopted at baptism); (3) rejection of OT; (4) rejection of orthodox sacraments and hierarchy; (5) special veneration of Paul; (6) rejection of icons. Eastern-medieval ancestor of Bogomil-Catharist dualist tradition through to Western Albigenses.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Paulicians: 7th-9th-c. eastern dualist sect; rejected OT, orthodox sacraments, icons; substantively gnostic-dualist; ancestral to Bogomils and Cathari.

expand to see more

The Paulicians' substantive corruption involved the standard dualist heretical package: rejection of the OT as the work of an evil creator-deity; docetic Christology denying real material incarnation; rejection of orthodox sacraments and church hierarchy. The pattern is substantively continuous with earlier Marcionite, Manichaean, and Gnostic movements and continuous forward into the Bogomil and Catharist movements of the late-medieval period. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the Paulicians as one historic link in the long chain of medieval dualist Christian-adjacent heresies. The distinctive Paulician feature is the special veneration of the apostle Paul: Paul's substantive antithesis between flesh and spirit, his strong language about the law's inadequacy for justification, his Christological emphasis on Christ crucified and risen rather than on the OT-historical narrative — these were misread by the Paulicians as supporting a dualist anti-OT theology that Paul himself decisively rejects (Romans 9:5; 11; 15:4; 2 Timothy 3:16). The Reformed-confessional reader receives Paul's apostolic theology in its substantive integration with the OT covenant-historical narrative.
